title: The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids
paragraphs: Once upon a time there was an old goat who had seven little kids, and she loved them as only a mother can. One day she needed to go into the forest to get food. She called all seven to her and said: “Dear children, I have to go into the forest. Watch out for the wolf. If he gets in, he will eat you all up—skin, hair and everything. The wretch often disguises himself, but you will know him at once by his rough voice and his black feet.” The kids answered: “Dear mother, we will take good care of ourselves. You can go without worrying.” So the old goat bleated and set off with an easy mind.

Before long, someone knocked at the door and called: “Open up, dear children! Your mother is here, and she has brought something for each of you.” But the little kids could tell by the rough voice that it was the wolf. “We won’t open the door,” they cried. “You are not our mother. She has a soft, sweet voice, and yours is rough. You are the wolf!” So the wolf went off to a shopkeeper and bought a big lump of chalk. He ate it, and it made his voice soft. Then he came back, knocked on the door, and called: “Open up, dear children, your mother is here and has brought something for each of you.” But the wolf had rested his black paws against the window, and the children saw them and cried: “We won’t open the door! Our mother doesn’t have black feet like yours. You are the wolf!” Next the wolf ran to a baker and said: “I’ve hurt my feet. Rub some dough over them for me.” When the baker had covered his feet with dough, the wolf ran to the miller and said: “Sprinkle some white flour on my feet for me.” The miller thought, “The wolf is planning to trick somebody,” and said no. But the wolf said: “If you don’t do it, I’ll eat you.” The miller got frightened and whitened his paws for him. That is just how people are.

So the wretch went to the door a third time, knocked, and said: “Open the door for me, children! Your dear little mother is home, and she has brought each of you something from the forest.” The little kids cried: “First show us your paws, so we can tell whether you are our dear little mother.” He pushed his paws in through the window, and when the kids saw that they were white, they believed everything he said and opened the door. And who walked in but the wolf! They were terrified and tried to hide. One jumped under the table, the second into the bed, the third into the stove, the fourth into the kitchen, the fifth into the cupboard, the sixth under the washbowl, and the seventh into the clock case. But the wolf found every one of them, and he did not stand on ceremony: one after another, he gulped them down his throat. Only the youngest, hiding in the clock case, he did not find. When the wolf had eaten his fill, he wandered off, lay down under a tree in the green meadow outside, and went to sleep. Soon afterward the old goat came back from the forest. Oh, what a sight she saw! The front door stood wide open. The table, chairs and benches were knocked over, the washbowl lay smashed to pieces, and the quilts and pillows had been dragged off the bed. She looked for her children, but they were nowhere. She called them by name, one after another, but nobody answered. At last, when she came to the youngest, a soft voice cried: “Dear mother, I’m in the clock case.” She lifted the kid out, and it told her that the wolf had come and eaten all the others. You can imagine how she wept over her poor children.

At last, in her grief, she went outside, and the youngest kid ran along with her. In the meadow they found the wolf lying by the tree, snoring so loudly that the branches shook. She looked him over from every side and saw that something was moving and struggling inside his bloated belly. “Oh, heavens,” she said, “could it be that my poor children, whom he swallowed for his supper, are still alive?” So the kid had to run home and fetch scissors, a needle and thread. The goat cut open the monster’s stomach, and she had hardly made the first cut when one little kid poked out its head. As she cut further, all six jumped out one after another. Every one was still alive and not hurt at all, because the monster had been so greedy that he had swallowed them whole. What joy there was! They hugged their dear mother and leaped about like a tailor at his wedding. But the mother said: “Now go and find some big stones, and we will fill the wicked beast’s belly with them while he is still asleep.” The seven kids dragged the stones over as fast as they could and stuffed as many into his belly as it would hold. Then the mother sewed him up again in a great hurry, so that he never noticed anything and never even stirred.

When the wolf had finally slept enough, he got to his feet. The stones in his belly had made him very thirsty, so he wanted to go to a well and drink. But as soon as he began to walk and move around, the stones in his belly knocked together and rattled. Then he cried:

“What’s rumbling and tumbling
Against my poor bones?
I thought it was six kids,
But it feels like big stones.”

And when he reached the well and bent over the water to drink, the heavy stones pulled him in, and he drowned miserably. When the seven kids saw it, they came running and shouted: “The wolf is dead! The wolf is dead!” And they danced for joy around the well with their mother.
